title: PIP for Arthritis: How to Build a Strong Application
meta_title: PIP for Arthritis: How to Build a Strong Application
meta_description: Build a PIP application for arthritis using GOV.UK rules: daily living and mobility scored separately, a 12-month test, and an evidence diary.
excerpt: How to describe daily living and mobility in a PIP application for arthritis, with the official points rules and a diary to take into the form.

content:
Quick answer: A strong PIP application describes how arthritis affects daily living and mobility, not the name of the diagnosis. GOV.UK says you can claim while working or if you have savings, and that you must expect the difficulties to last at least 12 months from when they started. Difficulties need to affect you most of the time, meaning more than half of the days over a 12-month period. Keep a diary, and use the claim guide for the practical steps.

Start in the right place. If you are still deciding whether to apply, read Can you get PIP for arthritis? That page is about eligibility and current rates. This page is about the application. The How to claim PIP for arthritis: step-by-step guide covers the phone call, the form and the assessment. The Printable PIP evidence diary is the place to record two to four weeks of daily living and mobility before you write the form.

What the application is judged on

GOV.UK explains that Personal Independence Payment can help with extra living costs if you have a long-term physical or mental health condition and you have difficulty with certain everyday tasks or with getting around because of that condition. There are two parts: a daily living part and a mobility part. You can get one or both. How much you get depends on how difficult you find those tasks, not on the diagnosis written on a clinic letter.

For each task, the Department for Work and Pensions looks at whether you can do it safely, how long it takes, and whether you need help from a person or from equipment. You must have difficulty most of the time. GOV.UK says that means you expect to have difficulty on more than half of the days over a 12-month period.

Who can claim

On the eligibility page, GOV.UK says you can get PIP if you are 16 or over, you have a long-term condition, you have difficulty with everyday tasks or getting around, and you expect those difficulties to last for at least 12 months from when they started. You also usually need to be under State Pension age to make a new claim. You can get PIP if you are working or have savings. In Scotland, working-age adults claim Adult Disability Payment instead. Northern Ireland has its own PIP service.

Points, in each part

Daily living and mobility are scored separately. The PIP regulations say that a score of at least 8 points for daily living activities is limited ability, and a score of at least 12 points is severely limited ability. The same 8-point and 12-point thresholds apply to mobility activities on their own. In plain terms, 8 to 11 points in one part is the standard rate of that part, and 12 or more is the enhanced rate of that part. Eight points overall, mixed across both parts, is not the same thing. Say which part a total belongs to.

The DWP assessment guide says a descriptor applies only if you can complete the activity reliably. The guide’s reliability section covers doing it safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and in a reasonable time. If you can dress once, but it takes much longer than it would for someone without your condition, or you could not do it again that day, describe that. The claim guide’s points section lists the activities.

What to put in the form

  • Describe a typical week, including better days and worse days, and how often each happens. GOV.UK looks at more than half of days, so a diary that only shows the worst hour is not the full picture.
  • Link pain, stiffness, fatigue and flares to a named activity: preparing food, washing, dressing, managing medicines, walking, or planning a journey.
  • Say whether you needed an aid, a prompt, or another person, and what happened if you tried without them.
  • Do not leave a relevant section blank. If something does not apply, say so.
  • Send supporting information you already have, such as clinic letters, a prescription list, or a note from someone who helps you. You do not have to pay for a new report in order to claim.

Start from the official route rather than from memory of an old form. GOV.UK: how to claim PIP is the current starting point for England and Wales. The evidence diary is a way to collect the examples the form asks for. It is not a DWP form.

If the decision is not what you expected

A decision letter explains the award. If you disagree, GOV.UK sets out how to ask for the decision to be looked at again, and then how to appeal. Our PIP appeal guide walks through that sequence. Deadlines are short, so read the letter as soon as it arrives.

What this page does not do

It does not predict an award, and it does not replace a welfare rights adviser. Citizens Advice and local welfare rights services can look at a form with you. Rules and rates change. Check GOV.UK before you rely on a figure, and use the dated rates section on the eligibility page only as a signpost to the official tables.

Frequently asked questions

Can I apply for PIP if I am still working?

Yes. GOV.UK says you can get PIP if you are working or have savings. The assessment looks at daily living and mobility, not at your job or your income.

How long do the difficulties need to last?

GOV.UK says you must expect the difficulties to last for at least 12 months from when they started, and that you must have difficulty on more than half of the days over a 12-month period. Describe the pattern, including flares, rather than one day.

What evidence should I gather?

A diary of daily living and mobility, clinic letters, a prescription list, and a short note from someone who helps you are the usual starting point. The assessment guide is about how activities are done reliably. The diary is there so you can show time, pain, aids and help. It does not guarantee an award.

Does 8 points mean the standard rate?

Only if those 8 to 11 points are all in one part. Daily living and mobility each have their own total. Twelve or more points in a part is the enhanced rate of that part. Eight points spread across both parts is not a standard-rate award.
